This module presents the Bhagavad Gita on its own terms. Here is how the Catholic Church speaks of it — you can explore it or leave it.

The Council says that in Hinduism people contemplate the divine mystery through a rich treasury of myth and searching philosophy, and seek release from the anguish of the human condition through ascetic practice, deep meditation, or taking refuge in God with love and trust.

The Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 2) teaches: “The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions.” Their ways of life and teaching often reflect a ray of the Truth that enlightens every person — yet the Church proclaims Christ, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), in whom people find the fullness of religious life.

Thy business is with the action only

column4: Dharma is the right order of things and one’s rightful duty within it; Arjuna’s crisis is a crisis of dharma.
The yoga of action: doing one’s duty with full effort while surrendering attachment to its results (2:47).
Loving devotion to God — for the Gita, the most direct path: “the devotee who loves Me is dear to Me” (12).
The path of knowledge: discerning the eternal Self from the changing body and world.
The Self that is not born and does not die, “not slain when the body is slain” (2:20).
Yoga means union and discipline — of action, devotion, knowledge and meditation.

column4: Krishna says he comes forth age after age (4:7–8). The Church proclaims one Incarnation, once for all: “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
Krishna accepts a leaf, a flower, fruit or water offered with devotion (9:26). Jesus praised the poor widow who gave two mites.
“Abandoning all duties, come unto Me alone for shelter” (18:66). Jesus says: “Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”
Do the work of today and leave its fruit with God: “Be not solicitous for tomorrow… seek ye first the kingdom of God.”
The Church also teaches that the soul is immortal (Catechism 366) — and hopes for the resurrection of the body.
Bhakti, loving devotion, finds its Christian echo here: “God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him.”
Arjuna sees a radiance like a thousand suns (11:12). On the mountain, the face of Jesus “did shine as the sun.”
